title: The realization-singular counit is a weak homotopy equivalence
statement: Use simplicial sets, geometric realization and the homotopy groups $\pi_r(-,t)$ of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], in a fixed universe large enough for the sets of continuous maps below. For a topological space $T$ let $\operatorname{Sing}(T)_n=\operatorname{Cont}(|\Delta^n|,T)$, with operators given by precomposition with the affine maps $|\alpha|$ of topological simplices. The evaluation map $$\varepsilon_T:|\operatorname{Sing}(T)|\to T,\qquad [\sigma,s]\mapsto\sigma(s)\quad(\sigma\in\operatorname{Sing}(T)_n,\ s\in|\Delta^n|),$$ is well defined, continuous and natural in continuous maps $T\to T'$. It induces a bijection from the path components of $|\operatorname{Sing}(T)|$ to those of $T$, and for every $r\geq1$ and every point $x\in|\operatorname{Sing}(T)|$ an isomorphism $\pi_r(|\operatorname{Sing}(T)|,x)\to\pi_r(T,\varepsilon_T(x))$, where $\pi_r(T,y)$ denotes homotopy classes relative to the boundary of continuous maps $([0,1]^r,\partial[0,1]^r)\to(T,y)$. No Hausdorff, compact generation, connectedness or nonemptiness assumption on $T$ is imposed.

proof.text: For each monotone map $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$, precomposition sends a singular $n$-simplex $\sigma:|\Delta^n|\to T$ to $\sigma\circ|\alpha|$. The identity and composition laws for the affine maps give the simplicial identities, so these sets and operators define $\operatorname{Sing}(T)$. Define $\varepsilon_T([\sigma,t])=\sigma(t)$. If a realization relation is generated by $((\operatorname{Sing}T)(\alpha)\sigma,t)\sim(\sigma,|\alpha|t)$, both representatives evaluate to $\sigma(|\alpha|t)$; hence the formula is well defined. It is continuous by the quotient universal property of the realization, and for a continuous $u:T\to T'$ one has $u\varepsilon_T=\varepsilon_{T'}|\operatorname{Sing}(u)|$, proving naturality. The fixed universe contains all these function sets by hypothesis.

source.place: Theorem 3.6.7, proof, printed p. 99; explicit evaluation, horn, representative and basepoint-transport argument.

proof.text: The singular simplicial set is Kan, without any hypothesis on $T$. A simplicial horn map $h:\Lambda_i^n\to\operatorname{Sing}(T)$ gives, by gluing its compatible simplex maps through the quotient presentation, a continuous map $\bar h:|\Lambda_i^n|\to T$; this uses only the quotient universal property and does not require $T$ to be a $k$-space. For $n\ge1$, [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits] identifies the pair $(|\Delta^n|,|\Lambda_i^n|)$ with $(D^{n-1}\times[0,1],D^{n-1}\times\{0\})$, so projection to the bottom factor supplies a continuous retraction $r:|\Delta^n|\to|\Lambda_i^n|$. The composite $\bar h r$ is a continuous simplex map whose restriction to the horn is $\bar h$; its restrictions to all faces therefore assemble to a simplicial filler of $h$. This also covers $n=1$ and both outer horns.

source.place: §3.1 adjunction and the realized horn-pair paragraph before Proposition 3.2.3; the retraction filler is written out here.

proof.text: Fix $t\in T$ and $n\ge1$. Let $Q_n=\Delta^n/\partial\Delta^n$, pointed at its collapsed boundary. A pointed simplicial map $Q_n\to\operatorname{Sing}(T)$ is equivalent to a continuous map $a:|\Delta^n|\to T$ that is constant at $t$ on $|\partial\Delta^n|$: in one direction glue the maps on simplices, and in the other send a simplex represented by $\alpha:[k]\to[n]$ to $a\circ|\alpha|$. These constructions are inverse by the realization relations. By [lem-coef-simplicial-realization-cylinder], the same correspondence with $Q_n\times\Delta^1$ identifies pointed simplicial homotopies with continuous homotopies $|\Delta^n|\times[0,1]\to T$ fixed on the boundary. After the standard radial homeomorphism between the simplex pair and the cube pair, this is a bijection $\Phi_n:\pi_n^s(\operatorname{Sing}(T),t)\to\pi_n(T,t)$, respecting concatenation in the first coordinate.

source.place: §3.4 simplicial homotopy groups and Theorem 3.6.7, printed pp. 97–99; representative and homotopy formulas supplied explicitly.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-kan-realization-serre] to the Kan complex $\operatorname{Sing}(T)$. At the vertex $c_t$ given by the constant singular $0$-simplex at $t$, realization induces an isomorphism $\rho_n:\pi_n^s(\operatorname{Sing}(T),c_t)\to\pi_n(|\operatorname{Sing}(T)|,c_t)$. For every representative $[a,z]$, $\varepsilon_T([a,z])=a(z)$, so $\varepsilon_{T,*}\rho_n=\Phi_n$. Step 3 makes $\Phi_n$ bijective, hence $\varepsilon_{T,*}$ is an isomorphism at $c_t$. The component assertion follows from the same node: vertices of $\operatorname{Sing}(T)$ are points of $T$ and its edges are exactly paths in $T$, while every point of a realization simplex is path connected to a vertex along a straight line; therefore evaluation induces a bijection on path components.

source.place: Proposition 3.6.3 and Theorem 3.6.7, printed pp. 97–99; evaluation on representatives and components expanded here.

proof.text: It remains to treat an arbitrary basepoint $y=[\sigma,z]\in|\operatorname{Sing}(T)|$. Choose a vertex $e_0\in|\Delta^m|$ of the simplex containing $z$, put $v=[\sigma,e_0]$, and let $\gamma(s)=[\sigma,(1-s)e_0+sz]$, a path from $v$ to $y$. Attach an interval at its endpoint to $|\operatorname{Sing}(T)|$ and to $T$ at $y$ and $\varepsilon_T(y)$, obtaining pointed spaces $E$ and $F$. Define $r_E,h_E:E\to|\operatorname{Sing}(T)|$ to be the identity on the original summand and respectively the constant map $y$ and the path $\gamma$ on the attached interval; define $r_F,h_F$ analogously using $\varepsilon_T\gamma$. The quotient universal property gives continuous maps. Sliding the attached interval into its endpoint gives a homotopy from $1_E$ to $i_Er_E$; sliding first to the endpoint and then along $\gamma$ gives a homotopy from $1_E$ to $i_Eh_E$, with the explicit two pieces $s\mapsto s+2a(1-s)$ for $0\le a\le1/2$ and $s\mapsto\gamma(1-(2a-1)(1-s))$ for $1/2\le a\le1$. The same formulas define the homotopies for $F$. Joint continuity follows by the compact-open currying theorem [lem-coef-compact-open-currying] for the compact interval and descent through the quotient.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed pp. 341–342; attached-interval basepoint transport and explicit homotopies.

proof.text: Define $\varepsilon^+:E\to F$ by $\varepsilon_T$ on the original summand and the identity on the attached interval. The quotient definitions give strict equalities $r_F\varepsilon^+=\varepsilon_T r_E$ and $h_F\varepsilon^+=\varepsilon_T h_E$. Each of $r_E,r_F,h_E,h_F$ is a homotopy equivalence by Step 5, so [lem-coef-homotopy-equivalence-weak] makes its induced map on every positive homotopy group an isomorphism at the attached endpoint. Step 4 gives that $\varepsilon_{T,*}$ is an isomorphism at $v$; the square for $h$ then gives that $(\varepsilon^+)_{*,0}$ is an isomorphism, and the square for $r$ gives that $\varepsilon_{T,*}$ is an isomorphism at $y$ by cancellation. The same cancellation with path components, together with Step 4, proves the component bijection globally.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed p. 342; homotopy equivalences and nonstationary basepoints.

proof.text: For $T=\varnothing$, both $\operatorname{Sing}(T)$ and its realization are empty, so the component map is the unique bijection and there are no based points. For nonempty $T$, Steps 1, 4 and 6 give a natural continuous evaluation map, a bijection on path components, and isomorphisms on every $\pi_r$ at every basepoint of its source. These are exactly the clauses claimed, with no Hausdorff, compact-generation, connectedness or nonemptiness assumption.
